newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. bank says hopes to reassess China dam project.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bank says hopes to reassess China dam project.

text.p: The U.S. Export-Import Bank hopes to reassess China's Three Gorges hydroelectric project to try to help U.S. exporters to win contracts to build the waterworks, an Ex-Im Bank official said on Thursday.

The bank's board of directors decided in 1996 it could not offer financing to China to purchase land-clearing equipment from the United States because of a lack of information about the environmental impact of the world's biggest water control project.

"There's a lot more to this project and I'm very hopeful Ex-Im Bank can get the material that it needs in order to assist in future contracts where we can contribute," said Annmarie Emmet, the bank's business development officer in China.

China is reviewing tenders from several foreign consortiums, but largely excluding the United States, to supply the first group of generating units for the project and will announce the winners this month, Chinese officials have said.
"We may have missed this round but we would like to be in on future contracts," Emmet said in an interview.

China is considering Siemens AG and GE Canada; Anglo-French group GEC-Alsthom NV; Swedish-Swiss Group ABB Asea Brown Boveri; a Russian consortium; a Japanese group; Impsa of Argentina and a Canadian unit of Westinghouse Electric Corp for the generators, official media has reported.

The Ex-Im Bank has asked the China Yangtze Three Gorges Development Corp to provide more information on the environmental impact of the project, including the potential impact of flooding areas with existing landfills, Emmet said.

The bank's approval of the project would clear the way for U.S. exporters to win valuable contracts to sell power generation equipment and other items to China with the help of Ex-Im Bank financing, she said.

Bank officials said last year there were questions about maintaining adequate water quality in the project reservoir, protecting ecological resources and preserving endangered species and the impact of the proposed resettlement of 1.3 million people.
"Anything that has to do with the power side, where the United States is quite good, we would hope that we would not be too late to get in on some of those types of contracts," Emmet said.
The huge Three Gorges hydropower and water conservation project, which would dam China's Yangtze River, is scheduled for completion in 2009.
China is currently the second largest recipient of Ex-Im Bank financing, receiving around $1 billion annually mainly in the areas of aircraft, petrochemicals and power equipment, she said.
"The reason for Ex-Im Bank's creation is to keep American exporters competitive, when they meet competition, and we do meet a lot of competition here in China," Emmet said.
"We would like to equalise the financing so the Chinese are purchasing on a quality basis and getting the technical products that they want."
